USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should hold the line on our existing tariff leverage but decline to trigger the Dec 15 escalation on consumer goods, and push to close and sign the Phase One deal now. Do not grant the tariff rollback China is demanding as a precondition, but use the credible threat and the imminent deadline to convert the already-agreed agricultural, IP and currency commitments into a signed agreement, keeping deeper structural issues (subsidies, tech transfer) for a Phase Two once Phase One is locked in.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat reading: this dispute is a mild opportunity, not an existential threat, for the United States. We own the escalation path — tariffs now cover roughly $360B of Chinese goods (timeline, 2019-05 through 2019-09 entries) — and China is making concessions (ag purchases, currency accord, tariff exemptions), not the reverse. The domestic economy is absorbing the shock: consumer sentiment rebounded from its August trough (89.8) to 99.3, industrial production is roughly flat, and the dollar is holding near 116 on the broad index (country_health, USA). The principal residual risks are self-inflicted — pushing the Dec 15 15% tariff on ~$160B of phones, laptops and toys would hit US consumers, retailers and tech supply chains at holiday peak and delay a deal we are positioned to win (web_search, CNBC 2019-12-10; Politico listing phones/laptops/footwear). Action stance: because we hold leverage and are near a favorable settlement, the optimal move is de-escalatory-but-not-concessive — defer the December tariffs to clear the path to a signed Phase One while preserving our tariff structure as leverage, rather than escalate into an outcome that hurts US consumers and invites renewed retaliation on US exports such as autos and agriculture (timeline 2019-08-23). This is consistent with a mild-opportunity threat reading driving a moderate negotiate stance.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating in good faith to lock in the Phase One deal and secure a rollback or postponement of the looming Dec 15 tariff, while holding existing retaliatory tariffs as leverage until terms are on paper. Do not escalate now: both sides are on the doorstep of an agreement intended to forestall the Dec 15 hike, and escalation would risk the near-term truce and be answered in kind. Keep pressing for relief on the Sept 1 tariffs and for the Dec 15 list to be taken off the table, without over-committing on purchases ahead of a signed text.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but moderate (threat_score +0.35), not existential. The US has imposed broad tariffs (List 3 at 25% on 2019-05-10; List 4A at 15% on 2019-09-01; List 4B ~$156-160B due Dec 15), placed Huawei and affiliates on the Entity List (2019-05-16), and designated China a currency manipulator (2019-08-05) — all genuine hits to export sectors and tech supply chains. Yet China's macro fundamentals remain firm at the decision date: reserves held at ~$3.13T (TRESEGCNM052N stable month-on-month), merchandise exports ~$211B and rising slightly (XTEXVA01CNM667S), CNY steady around 7.0 (EXCHUS 7.01, appreciating from ~7.15 in Sept), and industrial production growth 6-7% yoy (CHNPRINTO01IXPYM 106.9). There is also a clear de-escalation path: a Phase One deal was agreed in principle on 2019-10-11 (China to buy ~$40-50B US ag products/yr, IP and currency cited, Oct tariff hike delayed), and reporting through early December indicates both sides are close and expect to forestall the Dec 15 tariffs rather than let them bite. That combination — genuine costs but stable economy and an active truce path — justifies a mild stance (action_score +0.1, negotiate): the prudent move is to sustain talks and secure tariff relief rather than escalate into a fight China can absorb but would prefer to settle, especially with a 2020 US election and volatile US rhetoric in play.
